claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic NbMoTaW with a single-phase BCC structure.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical properties at temperatures up to 1600 °C.
Equiatomic NbMoTaW has limited room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of equiatomic NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally rather than established experimentally.
The proposed intervention is to add approximately 10 at.% V to equiatomic NbMoTaW during synthesis.
Vanadium addition will introduce local lattice distortion in the BCC matrix.
Vanadium addition may introduce uniformly distributed fine-scale precipitates or defect sinks in the BCC matrix.
Increased lattice distortion caused by vanadium can increase dislocation mobility at room temperature.
Greater room-temperature dislocation mobility will improve ductility.
The atomic size and diffusivity of vanadium may enhance recombination of irradiation-induced defects.
Enhanced defect recombination will reduce amorphization and helium blistering.
Approximately 10 at.% V can be added without significantly disrupting the BCC stability needed for high-temperature performance.
The V-modified alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile elongation than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will have lower room-temperature yield stress than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will exhibit lower irradiation-induced defect density and less phase instability than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will largely retain the high-temperature strength of untreated NbMoTaW up to 1600 °C.
The predicted irradiation benefit applies to helium-ion energies and fluences comparable to prior refractory-HEA studies.
Exceeding the vanadium solubility limit may cause phase segregation or precipitate formation that counteracts the proposed benefits.
